about.title: Hawthorne Workplace Injury Claims
about.longDescription: Getting hurt at work in Hawthorne can leave you with more questions than answers. Which system pays your medical bills? Can you do anything beyond filing a workers' compensation claim? The short answer under California law: workers' comp is normally your only route against your own employer, and it applies no matter who was at fault. But it is not always the end of the story. If someone outside your company contributed to the injury — a subcontractor on a shared job site near 120th Street, the owner of a building where you were making a delivery, the manufacturer of a machine that failed, or another driver who hit your work vehicle on Prairie Avenue — you may have a separate third-party claim with its own two-year deadline. That distinction matters in a city like this one. Hawthorne logged 328 injury collisions in 2025, with 416 people hurt, and some of those involved workers who were on the clock. LawProactive is a free service, not a law firm; we connect you with an independent attorney who can sort out which paths apply to you.

items.question: I deliver for a Hawthorne business and was hit by another driver on Rosecrans Avenue. Is that only a workers' comp case?
items.answer: Not necessarily. Because you were working, workers' compensation should cover your medical care and part of your lost wages regardless of fault. Since the other driver is a third party rather than your employer, though, you may also have a separate injury claim against that driver. Crashes in Hawthorne cluster on Friday afternoons between 3 and 5 p.m., a window when many delivery routes are still running, so this situation comes up more than people expect.

items.question: What happens if I didn't tell my employer right away?
items.answer: California asks you to report a workplace injury to your employer within 30 days. Reporting late can complicate a workers' comp claim, so it's worth doing as soon as you can, in writing if possible. Your employer cannot legally fire or punish you for reporting, and an attorney can explain your options if that has happened.

items.question: Can I sue my employer instead of going through workers' comp?
items.answer: In most cases, no. Workers' compensation is the exclusive remedy against an employer in California, even when the employer was careless. The exceptions involve outside parties — a property owner, an equipment manufacturer, a subcontractor on the same site, or another motorist — who may be pursued through a separate claim with a two-year deadline. Which path fits your situation is exactly what an independent attorney can help you sort out.
